slides.title: Who changed *ZTAIRLINE* at 2 AM?
slides.voiceover: Stop guessing who changed ZTAIRLINE at two AM. Last time we learned buffering. Now, logging data changes.
slides.spoken: Stop guessing who changed ZTAIRLINE at 2 AM. Last time we learned buffering. Now, logging data changes.

slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.heading: A value changed, *no trace*
slides.voiceover: Why? Someone changed the currency of LH from euro to dollar. Who? When? What was the old value? No log, no answer.
slides.spoken: Why? Someone changed the currency of LH from EUR to USD. Who? When? What was the old value? No log, no answer.

slides.heading: Tick *Log data changes*
slides.voiceover: The fix sits in technical settings. In SE11, click Technical Settings. Below data class and size category, tick Log data changes. Save and activate.
slides.spoken: The fix sits in technical settings. In SE11, click Technical Settings. Below data class and size category, tick Log data changes. Save and activate.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: *rec/client*
slides.body: rec/client = the profile parameter that switches table logging on for your clients.
slides.voiceover: But the flag alone logs nothing. The profile parameter rec client must switch logging on. It's a system setting your Basis team maintains.
slides.spoken: But the flag alone logs nothing. The profile parameter rec/client must switch logging on. It's a system setting your Basis team maintains.

slides.label: THE FIX
slides.heading: Every change *logged*
slides.voiceover: Now the same change writes an entry into DBTABLOG. Who did it, when, the old value, and the new one. Nothing is lost now.
slides.spoken: Now the same change writes an entry into DBTABLOG. Who did it, when, the old value, and the new one. Nothing is lost now.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: Read it in *SCU3*
slides.title: Table History · ZTAIRLINE
slides.voiceover: To read it, run SCU3 and pick your table. You see the user and the field. Then the old value, and the new one.
slides.spoken: To read it, run SCU3 and pick your table. You see the user and the field. Then the old value, and the new one.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Logging *everything*

good.title: Log customizing tables
good.sub: small, changed rarely, must be traceable

slides.voiceover: Common mistake: logging a big table like VBAK. Every change costs an extra write. Log small customizing tables instead.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: logging a big table like VBAK. Every change costs an extra write. Log small customizing tables instead.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Two switches, *one log*
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: the flag on the table, plus the profile parameter. Then read the log in SCU3.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: the flag on the table, plus the profile parameter. Then read the log in SCU3.

slides.title: *SELECT SINGLE* or UP TO 1 ROWS?
slides.voiceover: Stop failing the SELECT SINGLE interview question. SINGLE or UP TO one rows?
slides.spoken: Stop failing the SELECT SINGLE interview question. SINGLE or UP TO 1 ROWS?

slides.heading: The *interview* question

messages.text: Both read one row. So what's the difference?
SINGLE needs the full key. UP TO 1 ROWS takes the first row of a sorted result.

slides.voiceover: The question goes like this. Both read one row, so what's the difference? Here's the answer.
slides.spoken: The question goes like this. Both read one row, so what's the difference? Here's the answer.

slides.label: THE TRAP
slides.heading: Part of the key = *any row*
slides.voiceover: SELECT SINGLE wants the full key. Then you get exactly one row. Give it only part, like the customer? You get a random match. Not the newest. That's the trap.
slides.spoken: SELECT SINGLE wants the full key. Then you get exactly one row. Give it only part, like the customer? You get a random match. Not the newest. That's the trap.

slides.heading: The *latest* order
slides.code:
SELECT vbeln, erdat FROM vbak
  WHERE kunnr = @lv_kunnr
  ORDER BY erdat DESCENDING
  INTO @DATA(ls_order)
  UP TO 1 ROWS.
ENDSELECT.
slides.voiceover: Need the latest order of a customer? Sort by date, newest first, and take UP TO one rows. You get exactly that row.
slides.spoken: Need the latest order of a customer? Sort by date, newest first, and take UP TO 1 ROWS. You get exactly that row.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: ORDER BY with *SINGLE*
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: adding ORDER BY to SELECT SINGLE. SAP doesn't allow it. When the order matters, you decide with UP TO one rows.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: adding ORDER BY to SELECT SINGLE. SAP doesn't allow it. When the order matters, you decide with UP TO 1 ROWS.

slides.label: TAKEAWAY
slides.heading: Key or *order*?
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: full key, SELECT SINGLE. One row out of many? UP TO one rows, with ORDER BY.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: full key, SELECT SINGLE. One row out of many? UP TO 1 ROWS, with ORDER BY.

posts.caption:
Stop failing the SELECT SINGLE interview question: SINGLE or UP TO 1 ROWS?

A classic SAP ABAP interview question on reading one row from a database table.

1. SELECT SINGLE: use it with the full primary key, you get exactly one row
2. With only part of the key, SELECT SINGLE returns any matching row
3. UP TO 1 ROWS + ORDER BY: you decide which row, e.g. the latest order
4. ORDER BY can't be combined with SELECT SINGLE

Which one do you use most? Tell me in the comments.

slides.title: Country *XX* got into your table?
slides.voiceover: Stop letting one fake country into your table. Last time we learned logging data changes. Now, foreign keys.

slides.label: THE CHECK
slides.heading: Every value meets the *check table*
slides.voiceover: Why? Without a foreign key, the field takes anything. With one, SAP checks the value against T005 first. DE exists and passes. XX is rejected.
slides.spoken: Why? Without a foreign key, the field takes anything. With one, SAP checks the value against T005 first. DE exists and passes. XX is rejected.

slides.heading: Create the *foreign key*
slides.voiceover: Open the Entry help/check tab. Put the cursor on COUNTRY and click Foreign Keys. SE11 proposes T005, from the domain's value table.
slides.spoken: Open the Entry help/check tab. Put the cursor on COUNTRY and click Foreign Keys. SE11 proposes T005, from the domain's value table.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: The *field assignment*
slides.title: Create Foreign Key
slides.voiceover: In the dialog, SE11 pairs the key fields. Client with client, and LAND1 with your COUNTRY. Keep Check required ticked.
slides.spoken: In the dialog, SE11 pairs the key fields. Client with client, and LAND1 with your COUNTRY. Keep Check required ticked.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: INSERT *skips* the check
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: trusting it in code. The check runs on screens, like SM30. An INSERT from your program skips it. So check the value yourself.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: trusting it in code. The check runs on screens, like SM30. An INSERT from your program skips it. So check the value yourself.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: *Screens* check, code doesn't
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: a foreign key links your field to a check table. Screens check it. Your code has to check it too.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: a foreign key links your field to a check table. Screens check it. Your code has to check it too.

slides.title: *1:CN* in SE11, what does it mean?
slides.voiceover: Stop guessing what one to C N means. Last time we learned foreign keys. Now, cardinality.
slides.spoken: Stop guessing what 1:CN means. Last time we learned foreign keys. Now, cardinality.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: *Cardinality*
slides.body: Cardinality = how many rows on each side of a foreign key belong together.
slides.voiceover: Why? A foreign key links two tables. Cardinality says how many rows on each side belong together. You set it in the foreign key dialog.
slides.spoken: Why? A foreign key links two tables. Cardinality says how many rows on each side belong together. You set it in the foreign key dialog.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: Countries and *airlines*
slides.voiceover: Take T005 and ZTAIRLINE. Every airline has exactly one country. That's the one on the left. A country can have many airlines, or none. That's C N on the right.
slides.spoken: Take T005 and ZTAIRLINE. Every airline has exactly one country. That's the 1 on the left. A country can have many airlines, or none. That's CN on the right.

slides.label: LEFT SIDE
slides.heading: Left: *1* or *C*
slides.voiceover: The left side is one or C. One: every row has a match in the check table. C: the field may be empty, so no match.
slides.spoken: The left side is 1 or C. 1: every row has a match in the check table. C: the field may be empty, so no match.

slides.label: RIGHT SIDE
slides.heading: Right: *1, C, N, CN*
slides.title: Cardinality (right side)
slides.voiceover: The right side has four options. One: exactly one. C: zero or one. N: one or more. C N: any number, even zero.
slides.spoken: The right side has four options. 1: exactly one. C: zero or one. N: one or more. CN: any number, even zero.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Cardinality *won't block*

good.title: It documents the link
good.sub: the check table does the checking

slides.voiceover: Common mistake: expecting cardinality to block wrong data. It doesn't. It documents the link. The check table does the checking.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: expecting cardinality to block wrong data. It doesn't. It documents the link. The check table does the checking.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Left *1*, right *CN*
slides.body: 1:CN = each row has exactly one partner; a partner can have any number of rows.
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: one to C N. One country per airline. Any number of airlines per country.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: 1:CN. One country per airline. Any number of airlines per country.

posts.caption:
Stop guessing what 1:CN means.

SAP ABAP tables, Part 14 of 18: foreign key cardinality in SE11.

1. Cardinality = how many rows on each side of a foreign key belong together
2. Left side: 1 (always a match) or C (the field may be empty)
3. Right side: 1, C (zero or one), N (one or more), CN (any number)
4. Example: ZTAIRLINE to T005 is 1:CN
5. It documents the link, it doesn't block data
